The `source` array references a Git repository over HTTPS using the `git+https://` protocol, which is standard for `-git` AUR packages. The `sha256sums=('SKIP')` entry is typical for VCS-based packages and does not pose a risk during `--printsrcinfo`, as no sources are downloaded or verified at this stage. There is no evidence of malicious code execution, data exfiltration, or unsafe operations triggered merely by sourcing the PKGBUILD.

Therefore, running `makepkg --printsrcinfo` on this PKGBUILD is safe.
</details>

The PKGBUILD file defines a standard AUR package build process for `aurora-viewer-git`, a Rust-based Second Life viewer. It clones the source from the official GitHub repository (`https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer.git`), which aligns with the project's stated upstream. The `sha256sums=('SKIP')` is expected for VCS packages where checksums cannot be known in advance, and is a common and accepted practice in AUR packaging.

The build process uses `cargo build --release` to compile the Rust application, which is appropriate for the language and ecosystem. The modification of `CFLAGS` and `CXXFLAGS` to remove `-O2` is done to work around a known compatibility issue with the `aws-lc-sys` crate, which explicitly disables optimization for certain code; this is a legitimate build workaround, not obfuscated or malicious behavior. The package function installs binaries, desktop files, icons, and licenses to standard system locations, all with appropriate permissions.

No network operations, file manipulations, or executed commands deviate from standard packaging practices. There are no signs of data exfiltration, remote code execution, or unauthorized system modifications. The package depends only on common system libraries and tools required for GUI and multimedia functionality, consistent with the application's purpose.

This is a common and accepted practice, not a sign of malicious intent.

Materializing aurora-viewer-git from local mirror... Materialized aurora-viewer-git Analyzing aurora-viewer-git AUR package with deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash Performing initial audit of PKGBUILD to ensure that we can safely run `makepkg` LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD: UNSAFE
The PKGBUILD file is obfuscated by systematically replacing single and double quotation marks with HTML entity sequences (`'` for `'`, `"` for `"`). In shell, `&` is a job control operator. When `makepkg` sources this file during `--printsrcinfo`, the line `pkgdesc='A modern Second Life viewer, written from scratch in Rust (Vulkan)'` is **not** parsed as a plain variable assignment. Instead, the shell tokenizes it as the assignment `pkgdesc='A modern ... (Vulkan)`, followed by the background operator `&`, which then unconditionally tries to execute the token `apos;` as a top-level shell command. This fulfills the criteria for obfuscated code being used to inject shell syntax and execute unintended commands — the file is designed to be dangerous to source, not merely malformed. The remainder of the file triggers syntax errors on subsequent lines, but the pivotal command-injection attempt at global scope is already in play when `makepkg --printsrcinfo` evaluates the PKGBUILD.
pkgdesc='A modern Second Life viewer, written from scratch in Rust (Vulkan)' Obfuscated HTML entities inject shell commands at top-level scope. Second look for PKGBUILD (incontext): SAFE

The first verdict over‑reacted to the HTML entities. While the file is badly formed (every quote and angle bracket is HTML‑encoded with `'`, `"`, `<`, `>`), the consequences at top‑level sourcing are not genuinely malicious. When the shell attempts to parse lines such as `pkgdesc='A modern Second Life viewer … (Vulkan)'` it will break on the bare `&` control operators and try to run commands like `apos;` or `Vulkan`. These commands are not present on the system and will simply fail with “command not found”. None of the top‑level content contains a deliberate payload (no `curl|bash`, no `eval` of a decoded blob, no exfiltration). The fact that the file is obfuscated by HTML entity encoding is a packaging mistake, not a supply‑chain attack. The intended content behind the encoding is exactly the standard, innocent PKGBUILD for aurora‑viewer‑git. Nothing at the global scope will download, execute, or exfiltrate anything harmful.

Within the narrow `makepkg --printsrcinfo` gate, the file is safe — the shell may emit a flurry of error messages, but no malicious code is injected or executed. The function bodies (`pkgver()`, `build()`, `package()`) are not invoked, so any concerns inside them are out of scope for this step.
